top_strength: The proactive access probe was the best moment on the call and it is exactly the behavior that protects estimate accuracy. Alexander recognized the destination complex from prior jobs and surfaced the risk before it became a surprise on the bill: "we're actually pretty familiar with that complex but what we tend to find is that depending on what unit your apartment is going to be at. We can sometimes encounter like a pretty long walk there that can, that can add time." He then pinned it down with a second question — "do you know how long the walk will be on the ground floor from the truck to the elevator?" — and folded the answer into the estimate. He did the same with the storage stop, pulling drive times between all three addresses before adjusting the range. Rapport was genuine too: pulling the old contract and saying "got two of my favorites last time. You at MJ in Gerardo" landed well with a repeat customer, and he closed the booking in 8 minutes.
coaching_note: He booked the job without ever selling Einstein. Across 8 minutes the customer heard three dollar totals and nothing else — no hourly rate, no crew size, no No Worries coverage, no Meet Your Mover, no On-Time Guarantee, no no-deposit, no clock mechanics, and no Save Your Ass prep speech. A repeat customer is the easy excuse for skipping the pitch, but this one had a storage unit to empty and a seventh-floor destination, which is precisely the move where the prep speech pays for itself. The single highest-value fix: after "Did you want me to go ahead and secure the reservation for you there or?" and before the close, run the differentiator block and the prep speech. Second, the email close is the cheapest point on the scorecard and he left it on the table — "So I'll go ahead and send the confirmation email your way there" needs four more words asking Matthew to look it over and reply with any corrections.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and easy — the returning-customer callback ("got two of my favorites last time") and repeated genuine affirmations ("Okay, makes sense", "Yeah, that makes sense" when Matthew explained wanting to stop paying for storage) left the customer comfortable enough to close with "Thank you so much man"; held short of a 5 by heavy reliance on the same filler phrase ("Okay, good deal" appears roughly a dozen times) and no use of the customer's name until the goodbye.
